name: Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Fort Morgan Peninsula, Baldwin County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Primary, secondary, and tertiary Gulf dune zones; largest surviving population of the endangered Alabama Beach Mouse (Perdue Unit); nesting shorebirds, migrating songbird 'fallouts,' Gulf Fritillary butterflies, and nesting sea turtles.
special_note: Home to the single largest surviving population of the endangered Alabama Beach Mouse; the Pine Beach Trail crosses all three Gulf dune zones to the water.
best_time_of_year: Mid-March through April for peak spring songbird fallout events after Gulf-crossing storms (check 24-48 hrs after a front); June-July for sea turtle nest-laying (hatchlings emerge Aug-Oct).
scenic_highlights: The Pine Beach Trail boardwalk crosses pristine primary, secondary, and tertiary dune fields down to an open, undeveloped Gulf beach -- one of the last stretches of unbroken dune-to-surf scenery on the Alabama coast.
nearby_linkages: Perdido Key State Park / Gulf Islands National Seashore (Johnson Beach)

camping.notes: No campground on refuge; nearest developed camping is Gulf State Park, ~20 min away.

hike_rare_different_note: The Pine Beach Trail boardwalk crosses all three Gulf dune zones to an undeveloped beach, and the refuge protects the single largest surviving population of the endangered Alabama Beach Mouse -- a genuinely rare, intact barrier-dune ecosystem rather than a typical beach park.
must_see_trails: Pine Beach Trail (~3.3 mi round trip out-and-back, easy but sandy, to Gator Lake observation tower and Gulf beach); Jeff Friend Trail (~1 mi loop around Gator Lake, easier). Trail info at fws.gov/refuge/bon-secour.
overnight_town: Gulf Shores/Orange Beach, AL -- full range of lodging, restaurants, and services about 15-20 min away.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Gulf State Park
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Gulf Shores, Baldwin County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Shelby Lake (a drowned former stream) hosts freshwater fish, turtles, ducks, and American Alligators; maritime dune/scrub habitat once held the Alabama Beach Mouse, now locally extirpated by hurricanes.
special_note: One of the parks the author flags as 'particularly important for habitat preservation'; Shelby Lake is a sea-level-rise-flooded former stream that now hosts alligators.
best_time_of_year: Anytime for the trail network; alligators at Shelby Lake are most visible spring through fall (Apr-Oct) when active and basking, far less so in winter brumation.
scenic_highlights: Two miles of sugar-white Gulf beach, backdune views across Shelby Lake, and a 28-mile paved trail network winding through dunes and coastal pine forest to the Gulf State Park Pier.
nearby_linkages: Perdido Key State Park / Gulf Islands National Seashore (Johnson Beach)

camping.notes: 496 improved RV/tent sites plus a newer 104-site RV Resort; reservations recommended via alapark.com, especially in summer.
camping.name: Gulf State Park Campground

hike_rare_different_note: No rare-species headline hike, but Shelby Lake -- a sea-level-rise-drowned freshwater stream now hosting American Alligators a few hundred yards from the Gulf -- is a genuinely unusual sight, and the 28-mile paved Hugh S. Branyon Backcountry Trail network is one of the largest paved trail systems on the Gulf Coast.
notable_taxa: Alabama Beach Mouse (historic; locally extirpated by hurricanes)
must_see_trails: Hugh S. Branyon Backcountry Trail network (28+ mi paved, connects 9 named trails through dunes/pine flatwoods/marsh, easy); Gulf Oak Ridge Trail (3 mi); Rosemary Dunes Trail (1.6 mi). Trail map at alapark.com/parks/gulf-state-park.
overnight_town: n/a -- park has its own lodge, cabins, and 500+ site campground; Gulf Shores restaurants 10 min away.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Perdido Key State Park / Gulf Islands National Seashore (Johnson Beach)
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Perdido Key (Florida side of the Alabama-Florida line), Escambia County, Florida
flora_fauna: Barrier-island dune and scrub habitat; entire range of the endangered Perdido Key Beach Mouse.
special_note: Hosts the entire range of the endangered Perdido Key Beach Mouse, reintroduced here (2000) after repeated hurricane losses, most severely Hurricane Opal in 1995.
best_time_of_year: Anytime for the beach itself; March-August if you want a chance at nesting Snowy Plovers and beach-mouse activity (respect posted nesting closures); fall-spring for the coolest, least crowded visits.
access_note: Beach mouse populations are described as 'extremely low' as of the book's writing after repeated hurricane damage.
source_section: Perdido Key State Park / Gulf Islands National Seashore (Johnson Beach)
scenic_highlights: The longest stretch of undeveloped shoreline on the Gulf -- tall white dunes, turquoise water, and open views across Big Lagoon on the Florida side of Perdido Key.

camping.notes: No camping at Johnson Beach; developed camping at Big Lagoon State Park (FL, nearby) or Gulf State Park (AL, ~30 min).

hike_rare_different_note: The short Perdido Key Discovery Trail boardwalk is minor, but Johnson Beach itself is one of the last undeveloped barrier-island beaches on the northern Gulf and critical habitat for the endangered Perdido Key beach mouse and nesting shorebirds -- worth the trip for the beach, not a hike.
must_see_trails: Perdido Key Discovery Trail (~0.1-0.5 mi boardwalk loop, wheelchair accessible, wetland/salt marsh overlook); otherwise the visit is a ~1.4-mile beach walk from the two Johnson Beach parking areas. NPS info at nps.gov/guis.
overnight_town: Orange Beach, AL or Pensacola/Perdido Key, FL -- both ~15-20 min with full lodging and restaurants.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Dauphin Island & Dauphin Island Sea Lab
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Dauphin Island, Mobile County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Maritime forest famous as a spring migratory-bird 'fallout' hotspot; Dauphin Island Sea Lab runs the Mobile Manatees Sightings Network tracking West Indian Manatees along Alabama's coast.
special_note: Ranked among North America's top birding fallout sites during spring trans-Gulf migration.
best_time_of_year: Mid-March through early May for spring trans-Gulf migration, with the best 'fallout' concentrations 24-48 hours after a cold front or rain during that window.
access_note: The island (town, beaches, causeway) is publicly accessible; the Sea Lab itself is a research institution, not a visitor attraction.
source_section: Dauphin Island & Dauphin Island Sea Lab
scenic_highlights: Historic Fort Gaines overlooks the mouth of Mobile Bay, a public Gulf beach offers sunset views, and the Audubon Bird Sanctuary's maritime-forest boardwalk winds through dunes and swamp.

camping.notes: Public campground with RV/tent sites; reservations recommended during spring migration season.
camping.name: Dauphin Island Campground (town-run, near the Audubon Sanctuary)

hike_rare_different_note: Ranked among North America's top spring migratory 'fallout' sites -- after Gulf-crossing storms, exhausted songbirds pack the maritime forest in numbers rarely seen elsewhere; the Sea Lab's Estuarium and manatee-tracking program add a genuine research angle most parks lack.
notable_taxa: Wood-warblers during spring fallout (Hooded, Blackburnian, Cerulean)
West Indian Manatee (tracked by DISL's sightings network)
must_see_trails: Audubon Bird Sanctuary trail system (~3 mi of interlocking loops plus a boardwalk to Gaillard Lake observation deck, easy, through maritime forest/dune/swamp); Fort Gaines grounds for a separate historic walk. Map at townofdauphinisland.org.
overnight_town: n/a if staying on Dauphin Island itself (vacation rentals on-island); otherwise Mobile, AL, ~40 min, for more restaurant variety.

name: Weeks Bay Reserve
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Weeks Bay, Baldwin County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Salt marsh transitioning to freshwater grasses and East Gulf Coastal Plain Tidal Wooded Swamp (Bald Cypress, tupelo, Sweetbay).
special_note: A National Estuarine Research Reserve with an interpretive center enabling visitors to explore salt marshes, pine flatwoods, and a seepage bog.
best_time_of_year: April for white-topped pitcher plant flower and seepage-bog wildflower bloom.
scenic_highlights: A boardwalk trail crosses a pitcher-plant bog and tidal marsh to open views where the Fish and Magnolia Rivers empty into Weeks Bay.

camping.notes: No camping at the reserve itself; nearest options are Gulf State Park (~30 min) or private Fairhope-area campgrounds.

hike_rare_different_note: A compact, easy introduction to a pitcher-plant seepage bog and tidal marsh in one short walk -- pleasant for families but not a rare-species pilgrimage on its own; a nice, quick complement to Splinter Hill Bog's much larger pitcher-plant display.
must_see_trails: Pitcher Plant Bog Trail boardwalk (~0.5 mi, easy, interpretive signs, ends overlooking the Fish River); a second boardwalk leads out toward Weeks Bay. Combined trail system ~1.3 mi. Map available at the Weeks Bay Visitor Center, Hwy 98, Fairhope.
overnight_town: Fairhope, AL -- charming small town with real restaurant/lodging options, ~15 min away.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Splinter Hill Bog Preserve
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: near the Perdido River headwaters, Baldwin/Escambia County line, Alabama
flora_fauna: Alabama's most spectacular surviving shrub bog - carnivorous pitcher plants, Pine Barrens Treefrogs, and Henslow's Sparrows across 1,000+ acres of bog and longleaf woodland.
special_note: One of the best carnivorous-plant bog displays remaining in the Southeast.
best_time_of_year: Late March-April for peak pitcher-plant flower bloom; April into June for the bog's full pitcher (leaf) display.
access_note: Jointly held by TNC Alabama and Forever Wild; generally open for low-impact recreation, though the book does not describe formal trails.
scenic_highlights: One of the largest and showiest white-top pitcher plant bogs in the world -- spring blooms carpet the open seepage bog in red-and-white trumpet-shaped pitcher plants.
nearby_linkages: Conecuh National Forest & Blue Spring Wildlife Management Area

camping.notes: No camping on the preserve; nearest developed camping is Gulf State Park or Conecuh National Forest's Open Pond, both roughly 45-60 min.

hike_rare_different_note: One of the largest and showiest white-topped pitcher-plant bog displays in the world -- peak spring bloom genuinely rivals anything in the Southeast for carnivorous-plant diversity, with 12+ carnivorous species present on site.
must_see_trails: Pitcher Plant Loop (multi-use trail, 4+ mi, hikers/bikers/horses, counter-clockwise loop through the bog); parking off County Road 47 and Splinter Hill Road. No official published trail map found online -- confirm current access with Alabama Forever Wild or The Nature Conservancy before visiting.
overnight_town: Bay Minette or Foley, AL -- modest lodging options ~25-30 min; otherwise a day trip from Fairhope/Gulf Shores.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Gaillard Island (Mobile Bay)
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Mobile Bay, Alabama (offshore dredge-spoil island)
flora_fauna: Major seabird rookery - over 10,000 breeding Brown Pelicans in peak years, plus Laughing Gulls, Royal Terns, and more than 10 other aquatic bird species; several species breed nowhere else on the Alabama coast.
special_note: An artificial dredge-spoil island that became Alabama's primary coastal seabird rookery precisely because it is off-limits to people.
best_time_of_year: April through August for peak Brown Pelican nesting activity, viewable only by boat from a distance.
access_note: Explicitly described as 'off-limits to people' by design - this is precisely why the rookery has thrived. One of the book's 7 flagged non-visitable sites.
source_section: Gaillard Island (Mobile Bay)  —  not open to the public
scenic_highlights: A man-made dredge-spoil island surrounded by open Mobile Bay water on all sides; no public access (viewable only by boat), but a dramatic spectacle of thousands of nesting pelicans and terns on bare sand.

camping.notes: No camping on the island itself (no public access at all); the departure point, Historic Blakeley State Park, has its own campground nearby.

hike_rare_different_note: Not a hike at all -- it's a boat-only rookery, completely closed to foot access, hosting Alabama's largest brown pelican nesting colony (20,000+ birds) on a man-made dredge-spoil island; the only way to see it is a guided boat cruise.
must_see_trails: Not trail-based -- visit format is a guided boat cruise (about 3 hours, 9am-noon on scheduled dates) from the Five Rivers Delta Resource Center / Historic Blakeley State Park, viewing the rookery from the water around the island's perimeter. No independent access is possible.
overnight_town: n/a -- day trip from Mobile/Spanish Fort/Daphne area; cruise departs from the Five Rivers Delta Resource Center.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Haines Island Park & the Forever Wild Red Hills Tract
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Alabama River west of Franklin, Monroe County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Red Hills mesic slope forest with towering American Beech and Tulip-poplar; habitat for the Red Hills Salamander, Alabama's state amphibian and a Red Hills endemic.
special_note: Until recently the only public access point to Red Hills mesic slope forest, home to the endemic Red Hills Salamander.
best_time_of_year: Anytime for the forest hike; warm, rainy nights March-October give the best (still low) odds of spotting the nocturnal, burrow-dwelling Red Hills Salamander.
access_note: Haines Island Park has campsites, a boat launch, and a small single-car ferry; the adjacent 1,800-acre Forever Wild tract is explicitly open for hiking, hunting, and nature observation.
source_section: Haines Island Park & the Forever Wild Red Hills Tract
scenic_highlights: The Red Hills rise in wooded bluffs above the Alabama River; Haines Island park offers riverside and boat-launch views of the river bottomlands -- pleasant but low-key rather than dramatic.

photos.source: Wikimedia Commons (Library of Congress / photo by Carol M. Highsmith)

nearby_linkages: Fred T. Stimpson Wildlife Management Area
Conecuh National Forest & Blue Spring Wildlife Management Area

camping.notes: Primarily a day-use/boat-launch park on the Alabama River; could not verify an on-site developed campground in this pass -- confirm with the Army Corps of Engineers Mobile District before planning to camp.

hike_rare_different_note: The real draw is the Red Hills Salamander -- Alabama's state amphibian and a highly range-restricted endemic found almost nowhere else on Earth -- though the salamander itself is rarely seen (nocturnal, burrow-dwelling); the park/tract is one of the few public access points into its mesic slope forest habitat.
must_see_trails: No formal maintained hiking-trail system publicized; visit format is a riverside day-use area/boat launch at Haines Island Park plus Forever Wild Red Hills Tract access roads (primarily hunting/wildlife viewing rather than a marked trail network). Contact Alabama Forever Wild for current access points.
overnight_town: Monroeville, AL -- small-town lodging/restaurants, ~20-30 min; otherwise a day trip from the coast or Montgomery.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Roberta Case Pine Hills Preserve
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Autauga County, Alabama (Red Hills region; the book places it generally in the Monroe/Wilcox area)
flora_fauna: Secures one of the largest surviving populations of the Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant, nearly eliminated elsewhere by agriculture and fire suppression.
special_note: One of the last major strongholds of the Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant.
best_time_of_year: April-May for Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant bloom (visits require advance permission; no general public access).
access_note: No trails or public access described; a Nature Conservancy preserve not set up for casual visits. One of the book's 7 flagged non-visitable sites.
scenic_highlights: Rolling, deeply eroded sandhills and open, parklike sandhill longleaf savanna; the scenic draw is subtle -- airy pine stands and sandy ravines rather than any single dramatic overlook.

photos.source: The Nature Conservancy  —  photo by Harold E. Malde
photos.license: All rights reserved  —  personal use only, not for redistribution

camping.notes: No camping on preserve; access is limited due to fragile habitat (TNC asks visitors to call ahead about field trips). Nearest camping is Wind Creek State Park (~1 hr).

hike_rare_different_note: Protects one of the largest surviving populations of the Alabama Canebrake Pitcher Plant -- a species known from fewer than a dozen sites on Earth, all in two central Alabama counties -- a true single-species rarity, though the preserve's scenery itself (sandy ravines, open pine stands) is subtle rather than dramatic.
must_see_trails: No formal maintained trail system; The Nature Conservancy asks visitors to call ahead to arrange a guided field trip rather than dropping in. Not a typical hike-on-your-own destination.
overnight_town: Prattville/Montgomery, AL -- full lodging/restaurant options, ~20-30 min away.

name: Conecuh National Forest & Blue Spring Wildlife Management Area
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Covington County, Alabama (near the town of Wing)
flora_fauna: Some of Alabama's best remaining Longleaf Pine woodland; Red-cockaded Woodpecker nesting/roosting colonies; reintroduced Eastern Indigo Snakes, Gopher Tortoises, Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnakes, and Gopher Frogs; Blue Spring karst oasis.
special_note: Over 80,000 acres of longleaf pine woodland with active Red-cockaded Woodpecker nest trees and a dramatic karst spring oasis.
best_time_of_year: Spring (Mar-May) for Red-cockaded Woodpecker nesting activity and reptile/amphibian activity; Blue Spring itself is a year-round swim, warmest in summer.
source_section: Conecuh National Forest & Blue Spring WMA
scenic_highlights: Blue Spring is a strikingly clear, deep-blue artesian spring pool set in the forest -- a small but vivid highlight within otherwise flat longleaf pine flatwoods.
nearby_linkages: Solon Dixon Forestry Education Center & Blue Pond

camping.notes: Developed USFS campground on a 20-30 acre sinkhole pond; historically first-come, first-served -- confirm current reservation policy with the Forest Service.
camping.name: Open Pond Recreation Area Campground

hike_rare_different_note: One of the best remaining longleaf pine ecosystems in Alabama, with active Red-cockaded Woodpecker colonies and a genuinely rare reintroduced population of Eastern Indigo Snakes (North America's longest native snake); Blue Spring itself is a strikingly clear, deep-blue karst spring pool worth the stop.
must_see_trails: Blue Spring Loop (~5 mi, flat, longleaf savanna, trailhead off FR 335); Conecuh Trail (20-22.5 mi total: ~5 mi South Loop + ~13.5 mi North Loop + connector; backpacking permit required for overnight camping); Open Pond Trail (~1.75-2 mi loop around the pond). Forest map available via fs.usda.gov/r08/alabama.
overnight_town: Andalusia or Evergreen, AL -- modest lodging/restaurants ~20-30 min; or camp in-forest at Open Pond.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Solon Dixon Forestry Education Center & Blue Pond
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Covington County, Alabama (Dougherty Plain ecoregion)
flora_fauna: Blue Pond is an 80-foot-deep sinkhole pond over 350 feet wide that can drain suddenly when its clay plug fails - a Southern Coastal Plain Sinkhole ecosystem.
special_note: A dramatic, periodically self-draining sinkhole lake.
best_time_of_year: Anytime -- Blue Pond's turquoise color and occasional sudden draining are a year-round geological curiosity, not a seasonal event.
access_note: Primarily an Auburn University forestry education/research facility; not a general public park - visits likely require arrangement through Auburn.
source_section: Solon Dixon Forestry Education Center & Blue Pond
scenic_highlights: Blue Pond is a geological oddity -- a small sinkhole pond whose water glows an otherworldly turquoise-blue from suspended limestone particles, ringed by forest.
nearby_linkages: Conecuh National Forest & Blue Spring Wildlife Management Area

camping.notes: Solon Dixon Forestry Education Center is primarily an Auburn University teaching facility; public camping access not confirmed -- call ahead before visiting.

hike_rare_different_note: Blue Pond itself is the novelty -- an 80-foot-deep sinkhole lake that glows turquoise from suspended limestone particles and can drain suddenly when its clay plug fails; it's a geological curiosity more than a hiking or rare-species destination.
must_see_trails: No public hiking-trail network confirmed; Blue Pond is viewed via a short walk/overlook near the forestry center access road. This is primarily a teaching facility -- confirm public access with Auburn's School of Forestry and Wildlife Sciences before visiting.
overnight_town: Andalusia, AL -- closest real town with lodging/restaurants, ~20-30 min.

name: Old Cahawba Prairie Tract
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Dallas County, Alabama (Black Belt / Blackland Prairie, near Selma)
flora_fauna: Active tallgrass Blackland Prairie restoration using fire; wildflowers include Pinnate Prairie Coneflower, Old Cahaba Rosinweed, and Purple Prairie Clover.
special_note: One of very few places to see restored Black Belt (Blackland) prairie habitat in Alabama.
best_time_of_year: July-September for peak tallgrass Blackland Prairie wildflower and grass bloom.
access_note: Access not explicitly detailed by the book; treat as a TNC/Forever Wild tract generally open for hiking.
scenic_highlights: Alabama's most famous ghost town -- moss-draped live oaks, the lone standing Crocheron Columns of a burned antebellum mansion, and bluff-top views where the Cahaba meets the Alabama River.

camping.notes: No developed campground on the tract; Selma has nearby private campgrounds/RV parks.

hike_rare_different_note: One of the only places in Alabama to see restored tallgrass Blackland Prairie, plus the bonus of Alabama's most famous ghost town next door -- moss-draped oaks and the lone standing Crocheron Columns of a burned antebellum mansion.
must_see_trails: ~11.6 miles of multi-use trails (hiking/biking/horseback) through Black Belt prairie and pine-plantation forest; three parking areas off county roads from Selma. Adjacent Old Cahawba Archaeological Park (separately managed, historic ghost town) adds additional walking paths.
overnight_town: Selma, AL -- historic town with lodging/restaurants, ~10-15 min away.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Fred T. Stimpson Wildlife Management Area
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: ~10 miles south of Jackson, Clarke/Washington County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Contains a small disjunct outlier of Red Hills-type habitat geology, topography, and ecology, though outside the formal Buhrstone/Lime Hills ecoregion.
special_note: A geological curiosity - Red Hills-type habitat appearing well outside the main Red Hills ecoregion.
best_time_of_year: Anytime for the geology; fall-winter hunting season restricts general access, so check current WMA regulations before visiting.
source_section: Fred T. Stimpson Wildlife Management Area
scenic_highlights: Mostly flat, managed pine and hardwood bottomland with no signature overlooks; scenic appeal is quiet forest and wetland rather than dramatic terrain.

photos.source: Alabama Dept. of Conservation and Natural Resources (Outdoor Alabama)

nearby_linkages: Haines Island Park & the Forever Wild Red Hills Tract

camping.notes: Primarily a hunting-focused WMA; no developed public campground confirmed -- check outdooralabama.com for current status.

hike_rare_different_note: The genuine novelty is geological: an isolated outlier of Red Hills-type habitat appearing well outside the main Red Hills ecoregion, of interest mainly to naturalists; otherwise flat managed pine/hardwood bottomland without a standout trail or rare species to seek out.
must_see_trails: No dedicated public hiking-trail network found; access is mainly via WMA roads for hunting and wildlife viewing rather than a hike-focused destination.
overnight_town: Jackson, AL -- closest real town with basic lodging/restaurants, ~10 min away.

name: Moundville Archaeological Park
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: near Tuscaloosa, Hale County, Alabama (Black Warrior River)
flora_fauna: Not primarily a wildlife site; floodplain/riverine setting informs the park's discussion of pre-Columbian land management (nut-tree orchards, fire use, floodplain agriculture).
special_note: Preserves the second-largest Mississippian-period city ever discovered - 20 mounds, the largest 60 feet tall.
best_time_of_year: Anytime -- an archaeological site with no wildlife or bloom season; spring and fall give the most comfortable weather for climbing the mounds.
scenic_highlights: Twenty-nine earthen platform mounds rise from a broad bend of the Black Warrior River; climbing Mound A gives a sweeping view across the entire ceremonial plaza and surrounding river bottomland.

camping.notes: On-site campground with RV/tent sites; check moundville.museums.ua.edu for current reservation policy.
camping.name: Moundville Archaeological Park Campground

hike_rare_different_note: Not a hiking or rare-species destination -- it preserves the second-largest Mississippian-period city ever discovered, with 29 earthen platform mounds; climbing Mound A for the view across the ceremonial plaza and river bottomland is the signature 'hike,' paired with an excellent on-site museum.
notable_taxa: Black Warrior River floodplain hardwoods (nut-tree orchard legacy referenced in park interpretation)
must_see_trails: Not trail-based in the traditional sense -- a self-guided walking loop (~1-1.5 mi total) among the 29 mounds, plus the Jones Archaeological Museum. Climbing Mound A (the tallest, ~60 ft) is the highlight.
overnight_town: Tuscaloosa, AL -- full range of lodging/restaurants, ~15-20 min away.

name: Ruffner Mountain Nature Preserve
region: Ridge and Valley
location: Birmingham, Jefferson County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Cave Salamander in karst Salamander Cave near Hawk's View Overlook; roosting bats; dry calcareous forest on Red Mountain; exposed, tilted Chickamauga Limestone reef rock.
special_note: The book's opening geology case study; exposed limestone quarries show uplifted ancient reef rock.
best_time_of_year: Anytime for the quarry-geology hike; spring (Mar-May), especially after rain, gives the best chance of spotting Cave Salamanders.
scenic_highlights: Ridge-crest overlooks give skyline views of downtown Birmingham, plus dramatic reclaimed red-iron-ore quarry cliffs and pits along the Quarry Trail.
nearby_linkages: Turkey Creek Nature Preserve (Forever Wild Tract)

camping.notes: No camping on preserve; it's a day-use urban nature preserve.

hike_rare_different_note: A rare urban-geology hike -- the Quarry Trail winds through reclaimed 19th-century red-iron-ore quarry cliffs and pits with skyline views of downtown Birmingham, and Salamander Cave hosts Cave Salamanders in exposed karst limestone, all within city limits.
must_see_trails: Quarry Trail (moderate, past reclaimed iron-ore quarry cliffs/pits) to Hawk's View Overlook and Salamander Cave; additional ridge-crest trails give downtown Birmingham skyline views. Trail info via Jefferson County Greenways/Ruffner Mountain Nature Center.
overnight_town: n/a -- inside Birmingham, AL; full lodging/restaurants citywide.

name: Oak Mountain State Park
region: Ridge and Valley
location: near Pelham, Shelby County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Ridge-and-Valley oak forest over Double Oak Mountain; a studied Red-cockaded Woodpecker population.
special_note: Alabama's largest state park; used as the book's case study for Ridge-and-Valley oak forest ecology.
best_time_of_year: Spring (Apr-May) for wildflowers, Red-cockaded Woodpecker activity, and peak flow at Peavine Falls; fall for foliage.
scenic_highlights: Three lakes (Double Oak, Oak Mountain, Tranquility) ringed by forested ridgeline, plus Peavine Falls, a multi-tiered waterfall reached by a short, popular hike.
nearby_linkages: Turkey Creek Nature Preserve (Forever Wild Tract)

camping.notes: Developed campground plus cabins and glamping safari tents; reservations recommended via alapark.com, especially weekends.
camping.name: Oak Mountain State Park Campground

hike_rare_different_note: Alabama's largest state park (11,861 acres) with a studied Red-cockaded Woodpecker population and over 100 miles of trails -- including Peavine Falls, a popular multi-tiered waterfall hike, and the Red Trail, recognized on IMBA's Epic Rides list for mountain biking.
must_see_trails: Peavine Falls Trail (moderate, multi-tiered waterfall); Red Trail (IMBA Epic Ride, advanced mountain biking); Tree Top Nature Trail (easy elevated boardwalk). 100+ miles of trails total; map at alapark.com/parks/oak-mountain-state-park.
overnight_town: n/a -- park has its own campground/cabins; Pelham/Birmingham restaurants 10-15 min away.

name: Tannehill Ironworks Historic State Park
region: Ridge and Valley
location: near McCalla, Shelby/Tuscaloosa/Bibb county line, Alabama
flora_fauna: Natural areas expanded via Forever Wild funding adjoining the historic ironworks site; mixed Ridge-and-Valley forest.
special_note: Historic 19th-century ironworks site whose surrounding natural areas were expanded through Forever Wild conservation funding.
best_time_of_year: Anytime -- a living-history site; check the park's event calendar for living-history and reenactment weekends.
scenic_highlights: Restored 1830s stone blast-furnace ruins beside Roupes Creek, a shaded historic village of log cabins, and a scenic creekside walking trail through the ironworks grounds.

camping.notes: Developed campground with RV/tent sites; popular for Civil War reenactments and living-history weekends -- reserve ahead for event dates.
camping.name: Tannehill Ironworks Campground

name: Coldwater Mountain Tract & Coldwater Spring
region: Ridge and Valley

access_note: The Forever Wild mountain tract offers public recreation, but Coldwater Spring itself is primarily a tapped municipal water supply (up to half its flow withdrawn for Anniston) and is not developed as a wildlife-viewing destination - this is one of the book's 7 flagged limited-access features.
scenic_highlights: Rocky overlooks along the ridgeline (also a renowned mountain-bike trail system) give long views over the Coosa Valley; Coldwater Spring at the mountain's base is a clear blue karst spring.

must_see_trails: Coldwater Mountain Trail System (35+ miles of singletrack, multiple loops from beginner to expert, nationally recognized for mountain biking) with ridgeline overlooks of the Coosa Valley; trail map at coldwatermountain.com. best_time_of_year: Winter-spring (Dec-Apr) for the highest, most paddleable water levels on the Paint Rock River; spring for riparian wildflowers.

scenic_highlights: A clear, winding river framed by forested karst hills and bluffs, with caves and sinking streams throughout the Paint Rock Valley -- scenic but low-key, best appreciated by canoe or kayak.
nearby_linkages: Keel Mountain Preserve, Sharp Mountain Preserve & Bingham Mountain Preserve

name: Fern Cave National Wildlife Refuge
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: near the mouth of the Paint Rock valley, Jackson County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Protects escarpment slopes and a winter hibernaculum for endangered Gray Bats - one of the largest known Gray Bat hibernacula.
special_note: Protects a major Gray Bat hibernaculum; a single careless visit during hibernation can kill hundreds of bats.
best_time_of_year: Not applicable -- closed to the public to protect the wintering Gray Bat hibernaculum (bats present roughly Oct-Apr).

source_section: Fern Cave National Wildlife Refuge  —  not open to the public

notable_taxa: Gray Bat (largest wintering colony in the US, 1+ million bats)
must_see_trails: Fern Cave itself is closed to the public; other parts of the refuge may be open for limited activities, but no formal trail system is publicized. Check fws.gov/refuge/fern-cave for current access rules.
overnight_town: Scottsboro, AL -- closest real town, ~30-40 min.

name: Monte Sano State Park

overnight_town: n/a -- inside Huntsville, AL city limits; full lodging/restaurants everywhere nearby.

name: Sauta Cave National Wildlife Refuge
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)

name: William B. Bankhead National Forest & Sipsey Wilderness
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: Winston/Lawrence County, Alabama (Dissected Plateau ecoregion)
flora_fauna: A colossal Tulip-poplar (21 ft circumference, 153 ft tall); endemic Flattened Musk Turtle; rare Black Warrior Waterdog salamander (found in only 14 streams); dozens of waterfalls.
special_note: Contains Sipsey Wilderness, the first wilderness area designated in the Eastern US (1975), known as the 'land of a thousand waterfalls.'
best_time_of_year: Winter-spring (Dec-Apr) for maximum waterfall flow after rain; spring for wildflowers; fall for foliage.
access_note: Sipsey Wilderness is foot-traffic-only (no mechanized access) per Wilderness Act management.

camping.notes: Developed and primitive camping options throughout the forest; backcountry camping permitted in Sipsey Wilderness without a developed site -- check current Forest Service rules.

hike_rare_different_note: Home to Sipsey Wilderness, the first wilderness area designated in the Eastern US (1975) and known as the 'Land of a Thousand Waterfalls' -- old-growth hardwood gorges with state-champion trees and the rare Black Warrior Waterdog salamander, found in only 14 streams on Earth.

name: Dismals Canyon Conservatory
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: near Phil Campbell, Franklin County, Alabama (Dissected Plateau)
flora_fauna: 'Dismalites' - bioluminescent fungus-gnat larvae lighting canyon walls blue at night; a disjunct population of Eastern Hemlock and Black Birch far south of their main range.
special_note: One of the few places on Earth to see dismalites, a bioluminescent insect larva found almost nowhere else.
best_time_of_year: April-June for the peak dismalite display, with a smaller second peak in late September-early October; night tours typically run March through fall (closed in February) and are too warm/bright to be worthwhile after early summer dusk shifts.
access_note: Privately run ecotourism attraction; night dismalite tours require reservations.
scenic_highlights: A moss- and fern-draped sandstone canyon with waterfalls, grottoes, and giant boulders, famous after dark for the glowing 'dismalite' larvae that light up the canyon walls.

name: Chewacla State Park

location: near Auburn, Lee County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Longleaf woodland plus mesic, riparian, and dry oak-pine forest; distorted schist formations visible in stream valleys and an old quarry.
special_note: One of the southernmost extensions of the Piedmont physiographic province in the US, sitting right on the Fall Line.
best_time_of_year: Spring for the highest flow at Chewacla Falls and comfortable hiking; summer for the swimming lake; fall for foliage.
scenic_highlights: Chewacla Falls cascades over an exposed granite rock face into a swimming lake, with additional rock-slab 'Rock Garden' climbing bluffs and a scenic lakeside beach near Auburn.

camping.notes: 36 full-hookup sites and 10 primitive sites with shower facilities; six CCC-built stone cottages also available year-round. Reservations via alapark.com.

name: Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge
region: Interior Plateau & Tennessee River Valley (Highland Rim)
location: near Decatur, Limestone/Morgan/Lawrence counties, Alabama (spanning the Tennessee River)
flora_fauna: Nearly 50 mammal species, ~75 reptile/amphibian species, and 285 bird species along one of the most biodiverse rivers in North America.
special_note: The first wildlife refuge established on reservoir-management land (1938); hosts the annual Festival of the Cranes.
best_time_of_year: Mid-January for the annual Festival of the Cranes and peak overwintering Sandhill (and occasional Whooping) Crane numbers; broadly Nov-Feb for wintering waterfowl.
scenic_highlights: Broad Tennessee River wetlands and backwater views from the Beaverdam Boardwalk and Observation Building, especially scenic in winter when tens of thousands of migratory waterfowl and sandhill cranes gather.

camping.notes: No camping at the refuge; Decatur and nearby Point Mallard Park have camping options.

must_see_trails: Beaverdam Boardwalk and Observation Building (easy, wheelchair accessible, best in winter for waterfowl/crane viewing); refuge also has roughly 20 miles of nearby roads/trails plus 70 miles across the refuge open to hiking/biking outside the waterfowl-sanctuary closure season. name: Russell Cave National Monument
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: near Bridgeport, Jackson County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Eight bat species roost in and around the cave (six inside, two in surrounding forest); the spring-fed cave stream supports aquatic cave invertebrates; archaeological deposits record nearly 9,000 years of intermittent Native American use of the shelter.
special_note: Alabama's only other National Park Service unit besides Little River Canyon National Preserve; the mapped cave passage (7.2 miles) is the third-longest in Alabama, and the entrance shelter's artifact record is one of the most complete prehistoric occupation sequences in the Southeast.
best_time_of_year: Year-round -- the cave interior holds a stable temperature; spring and fall give the most comfortable surface-trail walking.
access_note: Free admission; visitors view the massive entrance shelter and museum via a short boardwalk and paved trail -- the deep cave passage itself is not open for general public entry.
scenic_highlights: An exceptionally large cave-shelter entrance -- used by Native Americans for almost 9,000 years -- opens onto a clear cave stream and sinkhole bluffs below Doran Cove; a paved trail and boardwalk let visitors walk right up into the entrance chamber.

camping.notes: No camping at the monument; nearest options are in the Scottsboro/Bridgeport area or at Monte Sano State Park (~1 hr).

hike_rare_different_note: Nearly 9,000 years of intermittent Native American occupation make this one of the most complete prehistoric occupation records in the Southeast, and the cave entrance itself -- part of a 7.2-mile mapped passage, the third-longest in Alabama -- is large enough to walk right into via a paved trail and boardwalk, even though you can't enter the deeper cave.
notable_taxa: Gray Bat and other cave-roosting bats (8 species total, 6 inside the cave)
must_see_trails: Paved trail and boardwalk leading up into the large cave-shelter entrance (easy, short); broader site has wildlife-viewing trails and is a stop on the Alabama Birding Trail. NPS info at nps.gov/ruca.
overnight_town: Scottsboro or Bridgeport, AL -- modest lodging/restaurants ~15-25 min; or Huntsville, ~1 hr, for more options.

name: Majestic Caverns (formerly DeSoto Caverns)
region: Piedmont & Talladega Mountains
location: Childersburg, Talladega County, Alabama
flora_fauna: A show cave in limestone deposited roughly 500 million years ago; the massive central chamber's dripstone formations (flowstone, stalactites, stalagmites) formed over about 3 million years -- geology rather than living biodiversity is the draw here.
special_note: Marked as the first officially recorded cave in the United States (1796); used by Native Americans for millennia (a 2,000-year-old Copena-culture burial was found here in 1965) and mined for saltpeter/gunpowder during the Civil War. Renamed from DeSoto Caverns to Majestic Caverns in 2022.
best_time_of_year: Year-round -- the cave interior holds a constant cool temperature regardless of season.
access_note: Privately owned, paid commercial attraction; guided cave tours plus above-ground maze, gem panning, and a cave light-and-sound show.
scenic_highlights: The Great Onyx Cathedral -- a single cave room roughly the size of a football field and about 12 stories tall -- is lined with some of the most concentrated onyx-marble stalactite and stalagmite formations in the country.

notable_taxa: Not a biodiversity site -- geology/archaeology only (Copena-culture artifacts, dripstone formations)
must_see_trails: Not trail-based -- guided cave tour through the Great Onyx Cathedral chamber and other passages; public tour hours Fri-Mon (check current schedule). Above-ground attractions include gemstone mining and a seasonal corn maze.

location: Fort Payne, DeKalb County, Alabama (base of Lookout Mountain)
flora_fauna: A large limestone cavern with an interior stream, at the base of Lookout Mountain; scientifically notable for preserved charcoal-drawn Cherokee syllabary inscriptions dated to 1828 found deep inside.
special_note: Contains the only known Cherokee syllabary writing documented inside any cave in the world, including a sacred message linked to the stickball game -- written just over a decade before the Cherokee Trail of Tears removal.
best_time_of_year: Anytime the site is open, but tours are inconsistent (by advance appointment, sometimes closed) -- confirm current status with Manitou Cave of Alabama before planning a visit.

scenic_highlights: A huge cavern entrance opens into chambers bearing 1828 Cherokee syllabary writing and English-language graffiti dating to 1814 -- one of the only caves anywhere combining dramatic cave scenery with an intact, deciphered Native American text.

name: Stephens Gap Cave (Southeastern Cave Conservancy Preserve)
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: near Woodville, Jackson County, Alabama
flora_fauna: A 143-foot vertical pit cave with twin 'keyhole' entrances -- a walk-in opening and a sheer skylight shaft -- where a seasonal waterfall pours through the sunlit opening into the chamber below; forested sinkhole terrain typical of the Paint Rock Valley karst.
special_note: One of the most photographed cave entrances in the Southeast: sunlight streams through the skylight pit opening and often carries a waterfall straight down into the cavern below.
best_time_of_year: After rain, for the waterfall pouring through the skylight pit; a free permit is required year-round for this technical vertical-caving destination.
access_note: A Southeastern Cave Conservancy (SCCi) preserve; a free permit (from permits.scci.org) and roughly an 0.8-mile hike are required to reach the rim. Viewing the walk-in entrance and rim is accessible to hikers, but descending the 143-foot pit requires vertical rope-caving skills and gear -- fatal falls have occurred, so this is not a casual descent.
scenic_highlights: A dramatic double 'keyhole' pit entrance where sunlight pours straight down through a sheer skylight shaft, often carrying a waterfall onto the cave floor 143 feet below -- one of the single most photographed cave scenes in the Southeast.

camping.notes: No camping at this small SCCi preserve; it's a day-visit vertical-caving site requiring a permit.

hike_rare_different_note: One of the most photographed cave entrances in the Southeast -- a dramatic double 'keyhole' pit where sunlight pours through a sheer skylight shaft, often carrying a waterfall 143 feet down onto the cave floor. This is a technical vertical-caving/rappelling destination, not a casual walk-in cave -- it requires proper gear and skills, and the county is listed as White-nose Syndrome positive, so decontamination protocols apply.
notable_taxa: Not a biodiversity site, though Jackson County caves are monitored for White-nose Syndrome in bats
must_see_trails: Not trail-based -- access is via a short walk to the pit entrance, then technical vertical caving/rappelling into the 143-ft shaft (requires an SCCi permit and proper vertical-caving equipment/skills). Contact the Southeastern Cave Conservancy (saveyourcaves.org) for permits and current access rules.
overnight_town: Scottsboro or Huntsville, AL -- Scottsboro closer (~20-30 min).

name: Noccalula Falls Park

location: Gadsden, Etowah County, Alabama (Lookout Mountain)
flora_fauna: Black Creek Gorge below the falls supports mesic forest and ferns; a cave sits directly behind the waterfall itself; the park's botanical garden displays over 25,000 azaleas.
special_note: Named for a Cherokee legend of a chief's daughter who leapt from the falls rather than marry a man chosen for her -- the falls were called Black Creek Falls before that name took hold.
best_time_of_year: After rain for maximum falls flow; late March-April for peak azalea bloom in the botanical gardens.
scenic_highlights: A 90-foot waterfall drops over a Lookout Mountain sandstone ledge into Black Creek Gorge, with trails winding past a cave behind the falls, an old pioneer homestead, and Civil War-era rock carvings.

camping.notes: On-site campground within the park; reservations via noccalulafallspark.com.
camping.name: Noccalula Falls Campground

hike_rare_different_note: A 90-foot waterfall with a cave directly behind it is a rare combination in Alabama, and the gorge trail also passes an old pioneer homestead and Civil War-era rock carvings -- genuinely more layered than a typical roadside waterfall stop, plus a botanical garden with over 25,000 azaleas.
notable_taxa: Mesic gorge ferns/understory plants typical of Black Creek Gorge; no single standout rare species documented
must_see_trails: Gorge trail below the falls (easy-moderate) passing behind the waterfall via the cave, the pioneer homestead, and Civil War-era rock carvings; botanical garden walking paths (25,000+ azaleas, best in spring). Trail info at noccalulafallspark.com.
overnight_town: n/a -- inside Gadsden, AL city limits; full lodging/restaurants nearby.

name: Horse Pens 40
region: Ridge and Valley
location: Steele, St. Clair County, Alabama (atop Chandler Mountain)
flora_fauna: 310-million-year-old Pottsville Formation sandstone eroded into polygonal rock faces, boulder fields, and natural stone amphitheaters; the mountain's springs and small caves support their own karst-adjacent plant and animal communities.
special_note: One of the premier bouldering destinations in the eastern US; climbing guides compare the sandstone's texture to France's Fontainebleau and England's gritstone areas.
best_time_of_year: Fall and spring for bouldering (cooler, higher-friction rock conditions); year-round for viewing the boulder-field rock formations.
access_note: Privately owned 40-acre nature park/campground; paid day-use and camping fees apply.
scenic_highlights: An otherworldly boulder field atop Chandler Mountain -- massive wind- and water-sculpted sandstone formations nicknamed 'Mushroom Rock,' 'Elephant Rock,' and 'The Stone Fort,' plus a sunset overlook across the surrounding valley.

camping.notes: On-site camping, popular during music festival weekends (book ahead for those dates); check horsepens40.com for current rates/reservations.
camping.name: Horse Pens 40 Campground

hike_rare_different_note: One of the premier bouldering destinations in the eastern US -- climbing guides compare the 310-million-year-old Pottsville Formation sandstone's texture to France's Fontainebleau and England's gritstone areas -- plus an otherworldly boulder field with formations nicknamed 'Mushroom Rock' and 'Elephant Rock.' Also hosts well-known bluegrass/music festivals.
notable_taxa: Not primarily a biodiversity site -- karst-adjacent spring/cave plant and animal communities, not individually documented
must_see_trails: Informal boulder-field walking paths among the sandstone formations (bouldering routes for climbers of all levels); sunset overlook across the valley. No formal distance-based hiking trail system -- this is primarily a bouldering/scrambling destination.
overnight_town: Steele or Ashville, AL -- modest lodging/restaurants ~10-20 min; or Gadsden, ~25-30 min.

name: Flagg Mountain (Weogufka State Forest)
region: Piedmont & Talladega Mountains
location: Weogufka State Forest, Coosa County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Old-growth longleaf pine and dry oak-pine ridge forest on the Appalachians' southernmost foothills; conservationists are actively working to restore and protect surrounding mountain longleaf stands.
special_note: The southernmost peak of the entire Appalachian Mountain chain (roughly 1,150 ft) and the southern terminus of the Pinhoti/Appalachian Trail hiking system; its 1930s CCC-built stone fire tower sat derelict for decades before a full restoration and 2025 rededication.
best_time_of_year: Fall for foliage and long-range ridge views from the fire tower; spring for wildflowers.
access_note: State forest; the restored fire tower and 1930s CCC cabins are open to hikers via a short walk/climb from a forest road.
scenic_highlights: A fully restored 1930s CCC stone-and-steel fire tower crowns the southernmost peak in the entire Appalachian chain, with 360-degree views across the Coosa River valley and the start of the Pinhoti Trail at its base.
nearby_linkages: Cheaha State Park, Cheaha Wilderness Area & Talladega National Forest
Coosa Wildlife Management Area & Coosa River Longleaf Hills Tract

camping.notes: Backcountry/primitive camping associated with the Pinhoti Trail terminus is reportedly available on Weogufka State Forest land -- confirm current rules and any lodge/bunkhouse options at the restored fire tower site before visiting.

hike_rare_different_note: The southernmost peak of the entire Appalachian Mountain chain and the southern terminus of the Pinhoti/Appalachian Trail hiking system -- a genuine through-hiker milestone, topped by a fully restored 1930s CCC stone fire tower (rededicated 2025) with 360-degree views across the Coosa River valley.
notable_taxa: Mountain Longleaf Pine (old-growth remnants, active restoration)
must_see_trails: Southern terminus of the Pinhoti Trail (which connects north to the Appalachian Trail in Georgia) begins at the base of Flagg Mountain; summit trail to the restored 1930s CCC fire tower. No official published map confirmed in this pass.
overnight_town: Sylacauga or Alexander City, AL -- modest lodging/restaurants ~25-35 min.

name: Natural Bridge Park (Natural Bridge of Alabama)
region: Southwestern Appalachians (Jackson County Mountains, Sand Mountain, Cumberland/Dissected Plateau)
location: Natural Bridge community, Winston County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Fern- and moss-draped sandstone canyon walls support shade-loving understory plants beneath a span of iron-ore-flecked sandstone.
special_note: Believed to be the longest natural bridge east of the Rocky Mountains (sources vary, roughly 148 feet long and 60 feet high).
best_time_of_year: Anytime -- a geological feature rather than a seasonal destination; after rain for a greener, mossier canyon; spring/fall for comfortable walking.
access_note: Small privately owned park with an entrance fee; a nature trail passes underneath and around the span, but visitors may not walk on top of the bridge itself.
scenic_highlights: A massive sandstone arch -- the longest natural bridge east of the Rockies -- spans a fern-draped ravine, with a short trail passing directly beneath the span and through boulder-strewn forest.
nearby_linkages: William B. Bankhead National Forest & Sipsey Wilderness

camping.notes: No camping at this small roadside park; nearest camping is in Bankhead National Forest, ~20-30 min.

hike_rare_different_note: Believed to be the longest natural bridge east of the Rocky Mountains -- a genuine geological rarity for the eastern US -- with a short trail passing directly beneath the massive iron-ore-flecked sandstone span through a fern-draped, boulder-strewn ravine.
notable_taxa: Fern/moss understory species typical of shaded sandstone canyon walls; no single standout rare species documented
must_see_trails: Short loop trail (well under 1 mi, easy) passing directly beneath the natural bridge span and through the surrounding boulder-strewn, fern-draped ravine. Privately operated -- confirm current hours/admission before visiting.
overnight_town: Haleyville or Double Springs, AL -- modest lodging/restaurants ~15-25 min.

name: Historic Blakeley State Park (Mobile-Tensaw Delta)
region: Coastal Alabama (Barrier Islands, Bays & Gulf Coast)
location: Spanish Fort, Baldwin County, Alabama (Mobile-Tensaw Delta)
flora_fauna: Sits within the Mobile-Tensaw Delta -- sometimes called 'America's Amazon' -- one of the most biodiverse river deltas in North America; old-growth bottomland hardwood and bald cypress-tupelo swamp shelter alligators, black bears, ospreys, and bald eagles, including a state-champion bald cypress near Bayou Jessamine.
special_note: Protects roughly 3,800-plus acres on the edge of the Mobile-Tensaw Delta, one of the largest and most intact river deltas remaining in the United States; also the site of the last major land battle of the Civil War (April 1865).
best_time_of_year: Winter for wintering Bald Eagles; spring and fall for comfortable hiking/paddling; alligators are most visible in warmer months (spring-fall).
scenic_highlights: Boardwalks and bluff-top trails overlook the Tensaw River and delta swamps, with the Bartram Canoe Trail threading through Spanish-moss-draped bald cypress and tupelo.
nearby_linkages: Mississippi Sandhill Crane National Wildlife Refuge (brief mention)

camping.notes: Fully furnished cabins, RV sites (up to 40 ft), tent camping (Harper, Bartram-improved, Delta-improved), horse-trailer camping, 'Squirrel's Nest' shelters, and group camping; reservations online via blakeleypark.com.
camping.name: Historic Blakeley State Park Campground

hike_rare_different_note: Sits on the edge of the Mobile-Tensaw Delta -- sometimes called 'America's Amazon,' one of the most biodiverse river deltas in North America -- with old-growth bottomland hardwood and bald cypress-tupelo swamp, plus the site of the last major land battle of the Civil War (April 1865). The combination of deep natural and Civil War history in one delta-edge park is genuinely distinctive.

must_see_trails: 20+ miles of walking/biking/horseback trails including the Boy Scout Civil War Hiking Trail and the USCT Heritage Trail; boardwalks and bluff-top trails overlook the Tensaw River and delta swamps. Kayaking into the delta swamps is also available. Trail info at blakeleypark.com.

name: Choctaw National Wildlife Refuge
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: near Jackson, Choctaw/Clarke County, Alabama (Tombigbee River)
flora_fauna: 4,218 acres of Tombigbee River bottomland lakes and sloughs; resident American Alligators, wintering waterfowl, nesting Wood Ducks, and Wood Storks that gather in backwater sloughs through the summer months.
special_note: Established in 1964 alongside the Coffeeville Lock and Dam; one of the few Alabama refuges with a resident alligator population listed as an explicit management purpose.
best_time_of_year: Winter for wintering waterfowl concentrations; summer for Wood Stork feeding and alligator activity in the backwater sloughs.
access_note: An information kiosk sits at the refuge's north end; a large portion of the refuge is accessible only by boat, and seasonal flooding can close refuge roads for days or weeks at a time.
scenic_highlights: Cypress-lined Tombigbee River sloughs and backwater lakes, with alligators sunning on logs and, in summer, wood storks working the shallows -- classic deep-South river-swamp scenery.
nearby_linkages: Haines Island Park & the Forever Wild Red Hills Tract
Fred T. Stimpson Wildlife Management Area

camping.notes: No camping at the refuge; check nearby Haines Island Park or private Jackson-area campgrounds.

hike_rare_different_note: One of the few Alabama refuges with a resident alligator population listed as an explicit management purpose -- classic deep-South cypress-lined river-slough scenery with alligators sunning on logs and, in summer, Wood Storks working the shallows.
notable_taxa: American Alligator (resident population, explicit management purpose)
must_see_trails: Refuge offers wildlife-watching, hunting, and fishing access (specific named trails not confirmed in this pass); best explored by vehicle/boat along the Tombigbee River sloughs and backwater lakes. Check fws.gov/refuge/choctaw for current access.
overnight_town: Jackson, AL -- closest real town with lodging/restaurants, ~15-20 min.

paddling.note: Likely paddle-able based on the water feature described; verify put-in/rental access locally.

name: Blue Springs State Park
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: Blue Springs, Barbour County, Alabama (near Clio)
flora_fauna: A constant ~68°F artesian spring feeds two concrete pools; the surrounding 103-acre park is mixed Coastal Plain pine-hardwood forest.
special_note: The 68°F artesian spring has drawn visitors since the 1890s, when the Whigham family built a hotel here promoting the spring's reputed healing properties; the state park was developed starting in 1963.
best_time_of_year: Summer for swimming comfort (the artesian spring itself stays a constant ~68 degrees F year-round); the annual Catfish Rodeo is also held here each summer.
access_note: No lifeguard on duty at the swimming pools.
scenic_highlights: A clear, cold artesian spring -- a constant 68°F year-round -- fills a pair of pools ringed by Coastal Plain forest; a quietly scenic, swimmable spring rather than a dramatic landscape.

camping.notes: 47 modern campsites (7 with sewer hookups) plus tent camping in modern and primitive areas, a bathhouse, and play areas; campfires allowed.
camping.name: Blue Springs State Park Campground

hike_rare_different_note: Honestly, no standout hike or rare species here -- the appeal is a constant 68-degree artesian spring (3,600 gallons/minute) that has drawn swimmers since the 1890s, filling two octagonal, sandy-bottomed pools rather than offering a hiking or wildlife destination.
notable_taxa: Not a biodiversity-focused site -- a swimmable artesian spring is the main draw
must_see_trails: Not trail-based -- the park's draw is swimming in the two spring-fed pools (constant 68F) rather than hiking; limited grounds for a short walk around the 103-acre park.
overnight_town: n/a -- park has its own campground; Clio/Eufaula, AL restaurants ~15-30 min for more variety.

name: Perry Lakes Park
region: Southeastern Plains, Red Hills & Black Belt Prairie
location: near Marion, Perry County, Alabama (Cahaba River floodplain)
flora_fauna: Four oxbow lakes and cypress-tupelo swamp left behind when the Cahaba River shifted course roughly 150 years ago; prime habitat for Wood Ducks, Barred Owls, Bald Eagles, and migrating songbirds including the Northern Parula.
special_note: A decommissioned Alabama Forestry Commission fire tower was relocated here and rebuilt by Auburn University's Rural Studio as a 100-foot birding tower -- giving a rare canopy-level view into a Black Belt swamp forest.
best_time_of_year: Spring and fall migration for songbirds viewed from the tower; late afternoon, year-round, for egrets and herons flying in to roost over the swamp.
access_note: Free, gated day-use park on AL-175; some trails/facilities have been slow to recover from past storm damage, so check current conditions before visiting.
scenic_highlights: A 100-foot rebuilt fire tower rises straight out of a cypress-tupelo swamp, putting visitors at canopy height with migrating songbirds and a sweeping view over the Cahaba River's oxbow lakes -- one of Alabama's most distinctive birding vantage points.

name: Wetumpka Impact Crater
region: Piedmont & Talladega Mountains
location: Wetumpka, Elmore County, Alabama
flora_fauna: Not primarily a biodiversity site -- the exposed crater rim supports mixed Piedmont/Coastal Plain transition forest, but the real feature here is geological rather than ecological.
special_note: Alabama's only confirmed meteorite impact structure: an asteroid or comet roughly 1,250 feet across struck here about 83-85 million years ago, leaving a crescent-shaped rim of hills rising up to 300 feet above the surrounding plain.
best_time_of_year: Year-round -- a geological feature with a downtown visitor/discovery center and self-guided public-viewpoint tour that work in any season.
access_note: The crater's best viewpoints are on private property, but the Wetumpka Impact Crater Commission maintains a self-guided tour of public viewpoints plus a downtown visitor/discovery center.
scenic_highlights: A nearly 5-mile-wide ring of crescent-shaped hills -- the eroded rim of an 83-million-year-old meteorite crater -- rises up to 300 feet above the Coosa River plain, visible from public roads and overlooks around Wetumpka.
nearby_linkages: Coosa Wildlife Management Area & Coosa River Longleaf Hills Tract

camping.notes: No camping associated with the crater site itself; nearest options are around Wetumpka/Montgomery or Wind Creek State Park (~30-40 min).

hike_rare_different_note: Alabama's only confirmed meteorite impact structure -- a genuine geological rarity. notable_taxa: Not a biodiversity site -- mixed Piedmont/Coastal Plain transition forest on the crater rim, no standout species documented

overnight_town: n/a -- inside/adjacent to Wetumpka, AL; Montgomery, AL restaurants/lodging ~20-25 min for more options.
